claims.text: Conventional stainless steel has native passive-film properties.
Laser surface alloying stainless steel with a corrosion-resistant HEA composition will improve its corrosion resistance.
Chromium, nickel, and possibly refractory elements incorporated through the HEA can stabilize protective oxides.
Laser surface alloying will produce a nanocrystalline or dual-phase modified surface layer.
The modified surface will develop a dense, uniform, chemically graded oxide scale during corrosive exposure.
Laser processing refines the surface microstructure.
Laser alloying alters surface chemistry by incorporating additional corrosion-resistant elements.
The refined microstructure and altered surface chemistry promote formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
The stable, adherent oxide layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species and reduces the corrosion rate.
Laser-alloyed stainless steel will have a lower corrosion current density than untreated stainless steel under identical aggressive conditions.
Laser-alloyed stainless steel will undergo less weight loss than untreated stainless steel under identical aggressive conditions.
The corrosion benefit depends on uniform surface alloying and appropriate laser-processing parameters.
Deleterious secondary phases can impair the corrosion benefit.
Nonuniform alloying or excessive dilution of alloying elements may negate the corrosion improvement.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement may vary with processing conditions and environmental severity.
